data.title: Middle East Eye: Miliband ‘looking at’ whether Palestine Action ban was sensible, argues mass arrests 'unintended'
data.author: Imran Mulla
data.summary:
Miliband ‘looking at’ whether Palestine Action ban was sensible, argues mass arrests 'unintended'
Submitted by
Imran Mulla
on
Tue, 09/29/2026 - 08:47
Foreign secretary's remarks at Labour conference come after arrests made at protest against ban on the direct action group
Supporters of the proscribed group Palestine Action gather to protest outside the conference venue on the first day of the annual Labour Party conference in Liverpool, north-west England, on 27 September 2026 (AFP)
Off
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the government is “looking at” whether the ban on Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation was politically sensible, arguing that the government had not intended for mass arrests to take place by implementing the proscription.
Miliband’s comments came at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool the day after the mass arrest of protesters against the ban outside the conference.
“I believe in the right to peaceful protest, I think that is important,” Miliband said in an interview on LBC on Tuesday.
Notably the foreign secretary avoided defending the ban on Palestine Action, which was introduced in the summer of 2025 under Keir Starmer’s premiership.
“On the specific issue of Palestine Action,” Miliband said, “there’s a case coming before the Supreme Court and so I’ll let that case play out, because I think it’s important that that court process takes its course.”
Pressed by interviewer Andrew Marr on whether he believed proscribing Palestine Action with “all those elderly people and vicars and grannies and so on" was politically sensible, Miliband responded: “I don’t think anyone’s intent was to have those people criminalised, but obviously the Supreme Court has got to look at this issue, and obviously it’s something we keep looking at as government.”
Speculation ban might be lifted
Miliband’s remarks have sparked speculation that the government might ultimately lift the ban on Palestine Action.

data.title: Middle East Eye: UAE confirms Netanyahu visit for first time, with no mention of regional wars
data.author: MEE staff

UAE confirms Netanyahu visit for first time, with no mention of regional wars
Submitted by
MEE staff
on

The visit follows reports that bin Zayed warned Netanyahu of a Hamas operation before 7 October
Emirati President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al-Nahyan in Berlin on 10 September 2026 (Ralf Hirschberger/AFP)
Off
The UAE has officially acknowledged hosting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for talks with President Mohammed bin Zayed on Sunday, its first such acknowledgement since establishing relations with Israel in 2020.
In a statement late on Monday, the Emirates News Agency said simply that bin Zayed "discussed with the Israeli prime minister the bilateral relations between the two countries and ways to strengthen and develop them".
The UAE released no official photograph of Sunday’s meeting. Its statement made no mention of the regional wars in which the UAE and Israel are involved - in occupied Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, Iran, Yemen and Sudan.
Sources in the UAE told Haaretz that bin Zayed greeted Netanyahu at the airport.
The meeting also made the front pages of the UAE’s state-owned Al-Bayan and Al-Ittihad newspapers, which simply reprinted the official statement.
In May, Netanyahu’s office blindsided the UAE by revealing that he had secretly visited the country at the height of the Israeli-US war on Iran.
The Emirati foreign ministry responded by saying its relations with Israel "are public" and "not based on non-transparent or unofficial arrangements".
"Any claims regarding unannounced visits or undisclosed arrangements are entirely unfounded unless officially announced by the relevant authorities in the UAE," the statement said.
'Moral support'
The latest meeting follows a Haaretz report earlier this month that bin Zayed had given Netanyahu advance warning of a Hamas attack before 7 October 2023.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Turkey’s $17bn fund scandal becomes a political crisis for Erdogan
data.author: Ragip Soylu
data.summary:
Turkey’s $17bn fund scandal becomes a political crisis for Erdogan
Submitted by
Ragip Soylu
on
Tue, 09/29/2026 - 10:22
President vows accountability as the liquidation of 130 investment funds exposes ties to Turkey’s ruling elite
A picture taken in Istanbul shows US dollar banknotes and Turkish lira banknotes, 27 January 2021 (Ozan Kose/AFP)
Off
A crisis involving Turkish investment funds accused of running Ponzi-like schemes has affected half a million people, with authorities ordering the liquidation of some 130 funds worth $17bn earlier this month.
Already historic in scale, the financial turmoil has quickly become a major political crisis for President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s administration, exposing a web of connections between the funds, their managers and the ruling elite.
The most prominent political casualty so far has been Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, a deputy head of the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) and family minister from 2016 to 2018. She resigned on Sunday after the opposition accused her of making substantial profits from share sales shortly before the funds crisis triggered a major stock market sell-off on 16 September.
Erdogan addressed the controversy on Monday, pledging to pursue those responsible for market manipulation and fraudulent trading schemes.
“Whoever lays a hand on the nation's rights, assets or legal interests will face us and the state,” he said.
The funds in question concentrated their holdings in illiquid stocks with low free floats, making their prices easier to inflate because relatively few shares were available for trading. For example, the Tera investment fund generated a return of over 1,500 percent over the past year, a figure that is totally illogical by any market calculation or method.
Authorities have set a six-month timeline to sell the funds’ assets and repay investors. But experts are pessimistic about how much investors will recover, with many unlikely to receive the inflated gains reflected in their holdings

data.title: Middle East Eye: Gaza officials warn of imminent 'humanitarian catastrophe' as winter approaches
data.author: Qazi Zaid
data.summary:
Gaza officials warn of imminent 'humanitarian catastrophe' as winter approaches
Gaza’s Government Media Office has accused Israel of violating its commitments under the Gaza ceasefire agreement, saying the continued violations have worsened the humanitarian crisis as the ceasefire approaches its first anniversary.
Israel had committed 5,147 violations that killed 1,421 Palestinians, injured 4,983 and caused the arrest of 198 people, the office said.
It also said 72,826 aid trucks had entered Gaza of an expected 210,600 under the agreement, while only 13,785 people had been allowed to travel in and out of the territory of an expected 35,000.
As winter approaches, the office warned of a “certain humanitarian catastrophe” as more than 1.5 million displaced Palestinians live in worn-out tents.
It said 162,000 of Gaza’s estimated 270,000 tents were already unusable and warned that more than 255 damaged buildings were in danger of collapse.
The office appealed to the international community and the UN agencies to intervene urgently, fully open Gaza’s crossings, facilitate medical evacuations and allow winter relief supplies into the territory.

In an interview with journalist Vince Coglianese, Vance said President Donald Trump had made clear that “there is a universe where we can strike a deal with Iran, but that requires the Iranians to behave”.
He said Washington’s approach would be based on Iranian actions rather than statements.
Vance said Iran’s leadership involved “a number of different constituencies”, including hardliners, conservatives, moderates and clerics.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Red Sea crisis: What missiles and drones do the Houthis have?
data.author: Daniel Tester
data.summary:
Red Sea crisis: What missiles and drones do the Houthis have?
Submitted by
Daniel Tester
on
Mon, 09/28/2026 - 13:57
The group have taken more territory on the north Yemen coast near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, allowing them to target shipping
A security guard in front of a huge image depicting a missile with "Palestine" written on its side in Sanaa, Yemen, in April 2026 (AFP)
On
A rapid offensive by Yemen’s Houthis has intensified the country’s civil war and caused chaos in global oil markets.
The group, which has controlled much of northern Yemen for over a decade, has seized fresh territory from the pro-government forces and threatened shipping traffic, notably that of Saudi Arabia, in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, the maritime chokepoint linking the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.
With few signs of military formality, the group has often been described in international media as a "ragtag fighting force".
But over the past two decades, the Houthis have evolved to use missiles and drones to stage attacks inside Yemen as well as against Israel, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, among others.
Much of the group’s arsenal has either been designed or supplied by Iran, which regards the force as a member of its Axis of Resistance, a network of allies that also includes Hamas and Hezbollah.
The Houthis have also acquired weapons, including decades-old Soviet-era tanks and helicopters, after victory on the battlefield, and recently seized US-supplied military vehicles captured from retreating Saudi-backed forces.
While the Houthis’ stockpile levels are unknown, it is possible to assemble a sense of their firepower and military capabilities.
Who are the Houthis and what’s going on in Yemen?
Officially called Ansar Allah (“helpers of God”), the Houthis were founded in 1994 by cleric Hussein al-Houthi. Rooted in Zaydi Shiaism, they want more autonomy for northern Yemen, where much of the country’s population is concentrated.

data.title: Middle East Eye: As the US pulls its forces out of Iraq, what happens to Iran-backed armed groups?
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
As the US pulls its forces out of Iraq, what happens to Iran-backed armed groups?
The US has announced the withdrawal of its forces from Iraq, 23 years after the invasion that overthrew Saddam Hussein.
The development has been hailed by the Iraqi government as a final return to "national sovereignty" after years of American involvement in the country.
"October 1 will be a new day in the course of the Iraqi state, with the country free of any foreign military presence and the completion of national sovereignty over its territory," Iraq's Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said in a statement.
His statement is not quite accurate - Turkey still maintains a military presence in the country, though it has also pledged to soon hand over its Bashiqa-Zilkan military base in northern Iraq to the government.
The end of the US presence in Iraq, the deadline for which was 30 September, had originally also been tied to the disarming of the extra-government armed groups that, since the overthrow of Saddam, have been among the most powerful forces in the country.

British PM Burnham says Labour will be ‘principled’ in securing two-state solution
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Tuesday that his party will continue to work towards a two-state solution in the Israel-Palestine conflict in his first speech at the Labour conference in Liverpool as leader.
“We will be principled in our leadership in securing a two-state solution between Israel and Palestine, as Ed Miliband has shown,” said Burnham, referring to the foreign secretary’s speech on Monday in which he called the suffering in the Palestinian territories “a stain on the conscience of the world”.
Burnham also said that the UK would “stand up to threats wherever they come from, whether Russia, Iran, or anywhere across the world”.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham delivers a speech on the third day of the annual Labour Party conference in Liverpool on 29 September 2026 (Oli Scarff/AFP)

data.title: Middle East Eye: Two Palestinians killed and others injured in Israeli strike, gunfire in Gaza
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
Two Palestinians killed and others injured in Israeli strike, gunfire in Gaza
An Israeli strike and gunfire killed two Palestinians and injured several others in Gaza on Tuesday, Wafa news reported.
Medical sources at Al-Shifa Hospital told Wafa that the bodies of two Palestinians and several casualties, including children, were brought to the hospital following an Israeli air strike that targeted an apartment in the al-Nasr neighbourhood, north of Gaza City.
Gaza's health ministry said earlier on Tuesday that one Palestinian had been killed and 13 others wounded in Israeli strikes in Gaza in the past 24 hours.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Trump says Iran conflict to end ‘very soon’
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
Trump says Iran conflict to end ‘very soon’
US President Donald Trump has said the conflict with Iran will be over “very soon”, causing oil prices to plummet.
During a speech in Washington, DC, unveiling a new AI-powered federal platform on Tuesday, Trump said Iran is “failing very badly” and reiterated that the country will “not have a nuclear weapon”.
“That’ll be over with very soon,” said the US president, referring to the conflict with Iran, adding that “oil prices are going to be tumbling down just like they were before I had to make that little excursion to the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
US President Donald Trump holds up an executive order after signing it during a launch event in Washington, DC, on 29 September 2026 (Kevin Dietsch/AFP)
